Flood zone map: find your FEMA flood zone by address

Type an address or use your location, put the pin on your building, and see the zone FEMA's own map shows there, with its map panel and the date it took effect.

Find your flood zone on FEMA's map →

Your address goes to the Census Bureau's address finder and the map point to FEMA's map service, not to this site.

FEMA's map, not an official determination. FEMA provides its flood map data "as is", with no guarantee of its accuracy.

What the zones mean

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards.

Each zone, with what it costs and what claims there paid: Zone AE · Zone X · Zone VE · Zone A · Zone AO · Zone AH · Zone D.

Must I buy flood insurance in my zone?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

If the zone looks wrong

An owner or renter who believes the property was put in a high-risk A or V zone by mistake, because of how the zone line was drawn against streets or other features, can send FEMA technical information and ask for a Letter of Map Amendment, which identifies the property to be excluded from the zone (44 CFR part 70). If you think a lender's high-risk-zone finding is wrong, you and the lender together can ask FEMA to review it within 45 days of the lender's notice; a fee applies (44 CFR §65.17).

What this tool cannot tell you

Your premium, whether your lender will require a policy, and anything FEMA's digital map does not cover. The zone shown is FEMA's map, not an official determination.
